svg.title: Artery, vein and capillary in transverse section
svg.desc: Transverse sections: an artery with a thick wall of three layers and a narrow round lumen, a vein of similar size with a thin wall and wide flattened lumen, and an enlarged capillary whose wall is one endothelial cell thick with a red blood cell in its lumen.

g.data-info: Outer layer of collagen fibres that gives strength and stops the artery over-stretching or bursting.

Thick layer of smooth muscle cells arranged in circles, with elastic fibres between them. Elastic fibres stretch and recoil to maintain pressure; smooth muscle changes the diameter (vasoconstriction and vasodilation).
A sheet of elastic tissue between the intima and media; it looks wavy in section because the artery recoils.
Innermost layer: a single layer of flattened endothelial cells on a basement membrane. Smooth, so blood flows with little friction.
Narrow and round. Blood flows here at high pressure.
The thickest layer of a vein: collagen fibres that support the thin wall.
Thin, with few smooth muscle cells and elastic fibres, because blood pressure in veins is low.
Endothelium on a basement membrane; in limb veins it folds inwards to form pocket valves (not seen in this section).
Wide lumen: low resistance to flow at low pressure. Often flattened in section because the thin wall collapses.
Thin layer of protein fibres supporting the endothelium; molecules filter through it.
The capillary wall is one flattened endothelial cell thick: the shortest possible diffusion distance.
The nucleus bulges into the lumen because the cell is so thin.
Red blood cells (about 7–8 µm) pass through in single file, close to the wall, so oxygen diffuses only a short distance.

svg.text: Artery and vein drawn to the same scale; the capillary is enlarged. Nuclei shown in purple.
